Toyota Motor Corporation: Q&A Summary of the Second-Quarter Financial Results Briefing for Investors for FY2027 Date & Time November 5, 2026 at 4:30pm-6:00pm (Japan) Speakers Yoichi Miyazaki, Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer Takanori Azuma, Chief Officer, Accounting Group Hiroyuki Ueda, Chief Officer, External & Public Affairs Group Q. Thank you for the structured explanation of your medium- to long-term direction. I have two questions. First, you discussed your approach to holding cash and announced a substantial cancellation of treasury shares. My understanding was that you previously retained these shares to maintain the flexibility to respond to potential future M&A opportunities. You appear to have a wide range of new businesses and initiatives you would like to pursue. Could you explain the role of M&A within Toyota, where you see a need for it, and whether your

emphasis has shifted toward developing businesses internally? How has your thinking changed? That is my first question. Second, including your comments at the media briefing, Executive Vice President Miyazaki sounded relatively confident about the business in China. Your market share appears to have bottomed out and perhaps started to recover, but I do not feel that your performance has improved sufficiently to justify greater confidence in the future. How are you analyzing the Chinese market, and where do you see a path to success? For example, do you intend to move further into lower-priced segments? Or has demand in those segments largely run its course, allowing you to see some traction with an approach more distinctive to Toyota? Could you explain your thinking in more detail? Those are my two questions. A.(Takanori Azuma) Thank you. I will answer your first question. Until now, we

have maintained treasury share holdings at approximately 20% of issued shares. In our discussions with investors, some pointed out that this level was weighing on the price of shares in circulation because of concerns about when the treasury shares might come onto the market. Taking into account factors such as the levels at other companies, we have revised our level from 20% to 15%. Although this is a substantial cancellation, our first step has been to review the level through communication with the market and with all of you, while also considering how we might use treasury shares going forward. The executive team is currently discussing how to use the treasury shares we hold. (Yoichi Miyazaki) To add to that, we discussed the appropriate level while listening to investors through our various exchanges. We are reducing the holdings, but a substantial amount remains. I expect we will

also be asked what we intend to do with those holdings. We need to ensure that we are prepared as we enter new businesses. There is also still room to consider the appropriate capital structure in the context of our relationships with various affiliated companies. With those considerations in mind, we would like to examine further what to do with the remaining shares. On your second question, regarding China, the launch of vehicles jointly developed with our local partners has enabled us to halt the decline in market share. We are also seeing signs of a

turnaround. That is the progress I am sensing. We are also making solid preparations for the vehicles we will develop next. I used the phrase “With China For China” in today’s presentation. Through our discussions with customers in China, we have learned that what they expect from Toyota is not the same vehicles that Chinese OEMs offer. We frequently hear that they want vehicles that retain the character of “Made in Japan” and “Made by Toyota.” We will learn thoroughly from China in manufacturing, but we have confirmed that the distinctive Toyota and Lexus driving character we have developed with our master driver still resonates in China. Working with our chief engineers in China, we will develop the Toyota vehicles that customers there want, following “With China For China.” With these preparations underway, I feel that we can turn the business around. Q. Thank you. Let me briefly

confirm one point regarding my first question. Is it correct to understand that the priority and potential for M&A are entirely separate from today’s capital allocation announcement and the cancellation of treasury shares? A.(Takanori Azuma) That is how we have been discussing it. Q. My first question may be a little early, but how should we think about the direction for next fiscal year? Operating income for this fiscal year is 3.9 trillion yen. Will next fiscal year be a year in which you try to reach 5 trillion yen again? Or, looking at the second-half plan and the substantial increase in input costs, will it be another year of offsetting cost increases and keeping operating income broadly flat? There are various other major factors, including volumes, the easing of supply constraints, and price increases. When considering next fiscal year and beyond, using this second half as a

starting point appears to imply a fairly low level. Could you explain how we should think about this? My second question concerns the capital allocation chart. I do not know the profit assumptions, but broadly speaking, net cash will decline by around 7 trillion yen to 8 trillion yen. In the absence of exceptional uses of funds, such as strategic investments including M&A, does the chart indicate that you will allocate more than 100% of net income to shareholder returns over the next 5 years? Could you explain the chart’s message in terms of the level of shareholder returns we should expect? Please also explain where adjustments would be made if, for example, profits were to increase or decrease. A.(Takanori Azuma) Thank you for your questions. At around the same time last year, investors also asked us about the difference between the first and second halves. Last fiscal year, the

difference in actual results was approximately 245 billion yen. This fiscal year, it is 480 billion yen. This is partly because the effects of materials related to the Middle East and the outcomes of negotiations with suppliers inevitably tend to fall in the second half. We have also revised our second-half exchange rate assumptions this time. That contributes to the difference between the first and second halves, making the gap larger than last fiscal year. Nevertheless, we are finally seeing a year-on-year increase. The impacts of the Middle East and tariffs are very substantial, but we intend to fully offset higher materials prices and recover as much of the Middle East and tariff impacts as possible. We will work with the aim of generating even 1 more yen and selling even 1 more vehicle. We still have the second half of this fiscal year ahead of us, so we are not yet in a position to
comment on next fiscal year. However, that is the approach we intend to take.

Q. I believe materials prices will increase costs by around 1.3 trillion yen this fiscal year. Based on what you are seeing in the second half, do you expect a similar increase next fiscal year? In particular, will electronic component and memory prices rise at the beginning of 2027? The possibility of further increases in the second half is also being raised. With that in mind, Mr. Azuma, were you talking about how to offset cost increases of a similar magnitude? Or were you suggesting that the increase might be somewhat smaller, potentially leaving a net positive effect? Could you clarify the nuance? A.(Takanori Azuma) I see two types of materials price increases. One is the increase in crude oil and aluminum prices resulting from the situation in the Middle East. We have included part of this under the Middle East impact. In May, we assumed a relatively large impact, but it has eased

somewhat. Meanwhile, we expect prices for memory chips, copper, steel, and other materials to continue rising. We have fully incorporated those effects into the second half. We cannot predict next fiscal year, but we need to prepare by improving how we work with suppliers and advancing cost reduction and improvement efforts. For impacts other than those related to the Middle East, our approach is to assume further increases and take the necessary measures. (Yoichi Miyazaki) To add to the first point, our arrangements with suppliers and the effects on crude oil, aluminum, and other materials affected by the Middle East tend to be weighted toward the second half. That is partly a consequence of the rules governing price revisions. Even including those effects, we have been able to offset this fiscal year’s materials price increases through marketing efforts and cost reductions. I see that

as significant progress this fiscal year. It is important that our underlying structure has not deteriorated from the previous fiscal year. At the same time, we are not satisfied with the current level of cost reductions. The figures also show that there is still much more we need to do. As we look toward next fiscal year, we would like to strengthen our company-wide cost reduction efforts further. If we do that, I believe we may begin to see the potential for a gradual recovery next fiscal year as well. On your second question, we want to steadily do what we believe in and have profits follow as a result. Our goal is to increase dividends in a stable and continuous manner. We prepared the chart with those considerations in mind. We would like to share further details as we make progress. While remaining mindful of the recent pace of dividend increases, we intend to steadily implement

measures that make shareholders feel, “I am glad I have held Toyota shares for the long term,” and “I want to continue holding them with confidence in the future.” Q. I have two questions. First, perhaps this was intentional, but I noticed that you did not include the figure of 20% ROE this time. Nevertheless, it appears that the total payout ratio will remain at a very high level. With equity of 38 trillion yen to 40 trillion yen, that would seem to imply a substantial level of net income. Although 20% ROE is your North Star, could you explain your thinking? My second question concerns robotics. I felt that you had shifted up a gear this time. Could you explain the background, including any technological breakthroughs? You also said that this business would have a high profit margin, so could you give us some indication of

its scale and the sales revenues envisaged here? A. (Yoichi Miyazaki) Regarding ROE, investors have told us that we should manage equity, the denominator, properly rather than looking only at profits and sales revenues, and that this is part of the CFO’s role. Taking those comments into account, the executive team has held repeated discussions about what we should do with both the numerator and denominator to improve ROE. Starting with the denominator, as I explained earlier, we have taken a further step toward bringing it to an appropriate level while balancing the capital needed for growth. As also pointed out, we would like to continue increasing the total payout ratio. We believe that continuing to do so will, as a result, bring equity, the denominator, to an appropriate level. Meanwhile, we will convert the cash we hold into assets through capital expenditures and research and

development. However, if that were merely a 1-to-1 exchange, there would be little point. As a business, we must generate returns greater than the funds we invest. To that end, we explore a wide range of future possibilities every day through Woven Capital, Toyota Ventures, and other channels. We are working to combine the early-stage technologies and ideas we identify with our existing technologies and turn them into businesses. Among those opportunities, we have become more confident that robotics is an area in which we can make considerable use of our strengths. We have been discussing this with Toyota Group companies. Rather than creating entirely new technologies from scratch, we feel that combining technologies we already possess could enable us to develop something highly competitive. Of course, we would like to turn this into a concrete business quickly. However, our trials in

our own factories show that simply installing robots is not enough. Unless a robot that currently performs 1 task can perform 3 or 4 tasks, there is little benefit in Toyota doing this. We are therefore aiming for versatile robots that can perform various tasks, just as people do. First, we want to develop and refine them thoroughly in our own factories, and eventually extend their use into everyday life. We are developing robots with people at the center, aiming for their presence beside us to feel entirely natural. We have been discussing how developing these new businesses and generating returns greater than the funds invested could also move the relationship between the numerator and denominator of ROE in the direction we seek. I expect new technologies to continue emerging. We would like to incorporate the technologies we identify through our exploration and commercialize them as

quickly as possible. We will first develop and refine them thoroughly in our factories. At that stage, we would very much like you to visit the genba (where work is happening) and see them for yourselves. Q. The materials state that substantial investment in factory automation, or FA, is expected across Toyota’s supply chain. This includes robots and various other future FA investments. When you say “substantial,” what scale do you envisage over, for example, the next 5 or 10 years? What would that investment include, including robots? I imagine that Toyota’s capital expenditures to achieve this scale of robot deployment will also be very substantial. Regarding investment to replace aging facilities, you have said for some time that plants such as Takaoka and Tsutsumi are already more than 50 years old and need to be addressed. Looking further ahead, how will you respond to issues such

as the Nankai Trough? Capital expenditures this fiscal year are just over 2 trillion yen. Over the next 5 or 10 years, what capital expenditure requirements do you envisage within your overall funding needs? My first question for Mr. Miyazaki concerns that scale. Second, do you currently have any production bottlenecks? Some media reports refer to difficulties securing rare earths, semiconductor shortages, severe labor shortages, and

aging facilities, among other issues. In Japan, for example, customers still have to wait half a year or 1 year for most vehicles, despite your efforts. It feels as though this has not improved at all over the past 2–3 years. How do you view that? There was a gathering to express appreciation for Mr. Okuda this morning. In the past, he often said that Toyota’s biggest problem was that its supply lines were overstretched. Looking at the current figures, I cannot help feeling that Toyota’s supply lines may still be overstretched today. Mr. Miyazaki, could you share your thoughts? A.(Takanori Azuma) I will address the first question before handing over to Mr. Miyazaki. Capital expenditures and research and development expenses total approximately 4.1 trillion yen this fiscal year. They were approximately 2.4 trillion yen 5 years ago, so they have increased by around 1.7 trillion yen over

those 5 years. We did not decide on every initiative at the outset and then increase spending accordingly. This is the result of annual discussions in which we have built up investment in areas where we believe we should invest firmly. Of course, some investment reflects the growth in the scale of the company. Meanwhile, approximately 1 trillion yen of the increase is strategic investment to develop future sources of earnings. We are allocating that investment to various fields, including quantum technologies and AI. At the current level, we expect approximately 22 trillion yen in capital expenditures and research and development expenses going forward. We want to preserve sufficient capacity to continue making these investments. We have not presented a specific amount for growth investment, but we intend to invest decisively in areas where we need to pursue future opportunities. That is

how we would like to use those funds. (Yoichi Miyazaki) I will answer the second question. Broadly speaking, the current bottlenecks are body-on-frame vehicles and hybrids. Customers are facing long waits, both in Japan and globally. Starting with body-on-frame vehicles, we still produce a large proportion in Japan, particularly Land Cruiser models. In some respects, our earlier assessment was insufficient. We expected demand for body-on-frame vehicles to decline as CO2 regulations became stricter worldwide. In fact, demand for vehicles that protect people’s lives and serve as work vehicles did not decline. As a result, we fell behind in expanding production capacity, and customers are still waiting. We are making various improvements, including the second line (new plant) in Texas, but we still need to rely partly on overtime and work on days off. We are planning domestic production of

14,000 vehicles per day from the second half of this year into next year, but production of body-on- frame vehicles is still not keeping up with demand. In addition to keeping customers waiting, I imagine investors would say, “Producing more would also contribute to profits.” We intend to take firm action here. We will reorganize production while also making use of investment to replace aging facilities. The other area is hybrids. We expect to reach around 5 million vehicles this fiscal year, but we have less than five inventory days in the United States, and lead times in Japan remain long. Reaching 5 million vehicles is not the end. We are expanding capacity with the next level in mind. Through these efforts, we will first build a business foundation that can reliably support a scale of 10 million vehicles, centered on hybrids. On top of that, we aim to add BEV growth without adversely
affecting the model mix. That is the business structure we would like to establish toward 2030. In doing so, we intend to identify and steadily resolve each bottleneck.

Q. How much investment will be required for robotics going forward? What scale of initial investment in robotics do you envisage? A. (Yoichi Miyazaki) Earlier, I said that we would make use of approximately 1 trillion yen in investment to replace aging facilities. That is not robot development spending. It is funding to actually introduce robots as factories replace aging facilities. For development of the robots themselves, we would first like to work within our existing development spending. We believe the hardware, or the body, could be developed at a lower cost than developing a vehicle itself. We also believe some elements can be shared with vehicles and production equipment. What remains uncertain is the brain. We are currently collecting video and other data, using it to train AI, and building our knowledge of the best approach. However, collecting data in the wrong way can lead

to extraordinary costs. Drawing on the knowledge we have gained through our work with external partners, we are also finding ways to train AI and accumulate data efficiently. It is difficult to estimate the costs that will be required as the data accumulates because we have not done this before. As CFO, my guidance has been to make this work within our existing development spending. However, we would like to assess it as we proceed. Q. Thank you for the very passionate presentation and materials. There are still some points I have not fully digested, so I would like to ask two questions. The first concerns the Asia/Global South slide. What particularly caught my attention was your statement that you would apply lessons from China elsewhere and use them to launch a new multi-pathway platform covering the A–C segments. Could you provide more detail, including the timing of its introduction

and the scale of the platform? Regarding lessons from China, the China section also refers to selecting suppliers based on competitiveness, so I imagine you intend to apply that approach elsewhere. In applying those lessons, what do you intend to preserve, and in which areas do you see no need to resist change? Could you also explain your procurement strategy? That is my first question on Asia and the Global South. My second question concerns robots. There are various types of robots, and, frankly, I do not yet fully understand them. However, regarding your strategy of introducing robots when replacing aging facilities, simply rebuilding an old factory would leave a single task as a single task. To enable what currently performs 1 task to perform 3, I believe you would need to change the vehicle body structure. In that sense, I take it that you are beginning to pursue a very proactive

strategy for changing vehicle body structures alongside your robotics strategy. A transition through 2040 sounds like perhaps the most proactive strategy among global mass-market manufacturers. Is that understanding correct, or am I letting my imagination run too far? Could you clarify this? (Yoichi Miyazaki) Thank you. I will address the first and second questions in turn. First, for IMV and the Hilux, we are working to procure parts within the Global South rather than supplying them from Japan. We would like to apply what we have learned in China to those efforts. Naturally, if a part made in China is the best choice for a particular vehicle, we will use it without hesitation. At the same time, we need to carefully consider the best sources of procurement

across the Global South as a whole. Previously, I explained here that we were dismantling Chinese vehicles and reviewing the cost of each component. In the first vehicle we jointly developed with a partner company at that time, Japanese suppliers accounted for only about 10% of sourcing. That brought home the severity of the situation facing both us and our Japanese suppliers. Since then, we have worked with suppliers to consider how to rebuild competitiveness. Through repeated cost reductions and cost improvements, the sourcing share rose to 30% for the second vehicle. For vehicles currently under consideration, it has reached 40 to 50%, and in some cases more than 50%. Applying that experience elsewhere will enable us to develop sufficiently competitive vehicles with the suppliers that have already helped us build supply chains in Asia and the Global South. We are becoming more

confident about that. We originally wanted to deliver this platform to customers as early as possible in 2029. However, given the recent situation in Asia, we cannot simply leave the timing there. I discussed this with Mr. Nakajima yesterday. While considering the balance with other models, we will examine whether we can bring it forward, even a little. Also, combining the A–C segments across Asia and the Global South would give us a scale of 1.5 million vehicles. We can bring together a large volume exceeding IMV as a single group, so we believe there is considerable potential for cost reductions, including through parts commonality. On your second question, you are correct. That is precisely why we entrusted the leadership of robotics to CPO Shiga. Under Mr. Shiga’s leadership, we will first consider the factory of the future. We will then consider vehicle structures suited to

production in that factory. If we are serious about automation, we need to reduce production processes, the number of items to be assembled, and ultimately the number of parts themselves. Otherwise, no number of robots will be enough. We need to consider not only robots, but also what makes a vehicle easy for robots to build, and use that as the starting point for considering the vehicle body structure itself. The division of responsibilities with suppliers will also change. Together with Toyota Group companies, including Denso, Aisin, and JTEKT, we will begin by considering what structure would be best. Those discussions have already started within the Toyota Group. I believe it is appropriate to be somewhat proactive in this area. We want to fully recognize our strengths and move forward decisively. If we appear to be falling behind, I hope you will give us another firm push. Q. My

first question concerns shareholder returns on page 29. You indicate shareholder returns of 11–14 trillion yen. Could you explain the thinking behind that? Does this include the share repurchases being conducted this fiscal year? If it does, share repurchases and shareholder returns this fiscal year could total as much as around 6 trillion yen. That would leave roughly 5 trillion yen to 8 trillion yen in returns from March 2028 onward, or around 1 trillion yen annually. I imagine dividends would be the main component, with share repurchases of at most around 1 trillion yen to 1.5 trillion yen. Is your approach therefore to focus on dividends and use share repurchases primarily to absorb the unwinding of cross-shareholdings? Or will you also actively repurchase shares to some extent beyond absorbing the unwinding of cross-shareholdings? Could you explain your thinking? That is my first

question. My second question concerns a point that caught my attention in the earlier discussion of next fiscal year. At the media briefing, you indicated a tariff impact of around 1.1 trillion yen this fiscal year. Do you see a path to gradually reducing that impact? I believe this fiscal year also includes one-time refunds and other items. Could the impact

therefore increase instead, or will it decline? Please explain how you view tariffs going forward. You have also presented measures to increase volumes toward 2030. I believe RAV4 volumes have fallen significantly. As RAV4 production ramps up fully from next year, do you see overall volumes beginning to emerge from the current period of stagnation starting next fiscal year? Could you give us a sense of next fiscal year in terms of tariffs and volumes? A.(Takanori Azuma) On your first question, let me explain the baseline of 11 trillion yen. Dividends currently total approximately 1.2 trillion yen annually, or approximately 6 trillion yen over 5 years. In addition, the baseline reflects our intention to continue increasing dividends in a stable and continuous manner, as well as share repurchases, including 3.7 trillion yen related to Toyota Industries, 1.3 trillion yen this fiscal year,

and the 300 billion yen announced today. With those elements incorporated, we have set 11 trillion yen as the baseline. How much we can add will depend on the funding priorities Mr. Miyazaki explained earlier. First, we need to generate solid profits, and then consider share repurchases. Because this will vary with future profit levels, we have presented a range of 11–14 trillion yen. Please view 11 trillion yen as the baseline reflecting stable and continuous dividend increases and the share repurchases we have already announced. On your second question, we expect the tariff impact to decline from the previous fiscal year to approximately 1.1 trillion yen this fiscal year. Some of you may have expected a larger decline, but increased exports from Japan have also expanded the scope of exposure to tariffs. At present, taking into account refunds of parts tariffs, we expect some degree of

impact to continue next year and beyond. However, we do not intend to accept 1.1 trillion yen as a fixed assumption. What matters is how we reduce it from here. For example, we will review parts logistics routes and ship directly to Mexico where there is no need to go through the United States. We will also reduce the underlying scope of tariff exposure by increasing local production, as with battery production in North Carolina. The transfer of production from Baja California to Texas also has a significant reduction effect in terms of both tariffs and logistics. By building on these efforts, we would like to work with our suppliers to determine how far we can reduce the impact, rather than treating 1.1 trillion yen as a given. (Yoichi Miyazaki) Regarding the RAV4, the changeover in Kentucky took place in April this year, so 2026 inevitably falls within the transition. We therefore plan

to move firmly into full production toward 2027. Q. I have two questions concerning the organizational restructuring. First, does your restructuring mean that functions such as corporate planning will continue to reside within the in-house companies rather than at the corporate level? You have changed the organizational groupings this time. Could you explain the background? Toyota has characteristically continued without a corporate planning function, so I would like to understand the thinking behind the new organization. My second question concerns your supplier policy. You mentioned earlier that the competitiveness of parts sourced in China has been improving. At one point, expectations for a Toyota Group reorganization rose considerably, but my impression is that they have eased somewhat recently. Mr. Azuma, you have headed human resources and accounting, and will now head a regional
group. Having followed these areas throughout, how do you view them? Could

you share your impression of Toyota’s current supplier structure? Those are my two questions. A. (Yoichi Miyazaki) As I explained today, one reason behind the restructuring is our desire to place people development at the center as we pursue various initiatives. Another is our focus on the genba. There will be further explanation on this later, but we reconsidered how administrative functions should operate to advance the challenges undertaken by the genba rather than getting in their way. Toyota has distinctive approaches: “kaizen” (continuous improvement) in production, “Ever-better Cars” in development, and “Best-in-Town” in regional operations. Administrative functions naturally also have important roles, including cost reduction and managing the figures. However, if Toyota is doing this, perhaps there should be a distinctly Toyota approach that goes beyond ordinary administration.

Our discussions led to the “management through hands and eyes” approach I explained today. When the genba takes on something new, these functions should do more than oversee it. They should actively support it. We believe having that capability will help develop people and strengthen the genba. We have not done this before either. However, as team members ask themselves, “What should we do?”, a Toyota approach to this form of supportive management may emerge. That was also part of our thinking behind the organizational changes. For regions that require more detailed attention than before, such as India and the areas to its west, we are separating groups to establish a structure that allows more focused consideration. Meanwhile, we do not have a large organization for what is generally called corporate planning. Twice a week, the executive team meets for around one and a half hours to

discuss issues and determine the direction there and then. Rather than bringing large volumes of materials to a monthly corporate planning meeting to make decisions, as in the past, the relevant people bring matters requiring consultation directly to the meeting, and we make quick decisions. First, decide and act. If we get something wrong, adjust. That is also something we have learned from Chairman Toyoda. I see the executive meeting itself as our corporate planning meeting. We bring in feedback from the genba in a timely manner and resolve problems as they arise. That is how we would like to continue managing the company. (Takanori Azuma) On the first point, when we moved to the in-house company system in 2016, we placed functions such as accounting, human resources, production engineering, and cost planning within each in- house company. At the time, we made a substantial shift

toward the in-house companies. As we operated under that structure, however, we came to recognize again the benefits of keeping functions together for people development and company-wide strategic thinking. This year, we therefore brought production-related administrative functions back together under Mr. Shiga. Of course, we are doing this while retaining personnel responsible for these functions within each in-house company. We also reinstated the Cost Planning Division to regain its strengths. However, instead of returning it to headquarters, we placed it directly under the CTO in the engineering organization. When people are dispersed across in-house companies, it inevitably becomes more difficult to develop them through mutual teaching and learning. Since September, we have also consolidated accounting and human resources functions within the Technical Support Division. Having once
swung the pendulum from a functional organization toward the in-house company system, we are now bringing it back somewhat. We want to retain the benefits of the in-house

company system while regaining the strengths that functional organizations offered in people development, expertise, and company-wide optimization. We are adjusting that balance now. We are currently putting in place a structure in which those specialist functions can firmly support the executive team. (Yoichi Miyazaki) On your second question, regarding procurement policy, electrification was originally a major trigger for this discussion. As electrification advances, some suppliers, particularly those focused on parts for conventional vehicles, will be significantly affected. The discussion began with the question of whether that made supply chain restructuring necessary. Our perspective has now shifted somewhat. Looking at the vertical integration of Chinese manufacturers and Tesla, and then reviewing our own procurement, we see individual parts moving back and forth among Toyota

Group companies before finally reaching Toyota. That makes us stop and ask, “Each time, we are buying and selling with selling, general and administrative expenses and profit added, are we not?” To improve cost competitiveness further, perhaps we need to review the division of responsibilities itself: for example, making Company A responsible for one component and consolidating another at Company B. Those are the discussions we are having now. Furthermore, as pointed out earlier, we need to reduce the number of parts and assembly work hours, changing the vehicle body structure and component configuration themselves to achieve that. If we go that far, I believe a review of the division of responsibilities and structure with suppliers will be unavoidable. From the outside, the discussion may appear to have cooled somewhat. Internally, however, the opposite is true. We are discussing it as

a very active issue. Q. Thank you for today’s presentation. I have two questions. First, regarding your vision for fiscal 2030, the capital allocation explanation gave me a general sense of your thinking on equity. I would also like a clearer sense of your approach to profits. My understanding is that operating income this fiscal year is approximately 3.9 trillion yen, comprising just over 2 trillion yen from the value chain and just under 2 trillion yen from new vehicle sales. You indicated a value chain profit scale of 3 trillion yen in 2030. How much profit would you envisage from new vehicles at that point? Would the split still be roughly half and half, with new vehicle profits of around 3 trillion yen? You have also indicated preparations for production of 12 million vehicles toward 2030. Taking that into account, could you explain how you intend to translate this into profits?

That is my first question. Second, regarding the earlier China slide, unless I misread the pie chart, it appeared that sourced vehicles would account for around three-quarters of sales in 2030. That strikes me as a fairly bullish view. Naturally, I do not think joint-venture models alone would account for that entire amount. Are you seeing a much clearer path to success? Could you share your sense of progress in China as you look toward 2030? Thank you. A. (Yoichi Miyazaki) Regarding the figures, I believe they should emerge as the result of doing what we need to do, rather than pursuing the numbers themselves. We would like to keep building on our efforts so that, ultimately, we achieve the figures we have presented. On the value chain, I tell our team members, “There is still plenty of room to develop, and many areas to explore further.” However, the purpose is not simply to make
money. It is to extend our relationships with the customers who choose Toyota vehicles. That is why we want to explore

those opportunities. Of course, there are limits to what we can do at once. We are therefore discussing maintaining growth of around 150 billion yen annually as a first step. We believe this is fully achievable if we increase the number of vehicles in use, improve our customer retention rate, and extend the duration of our customer relationships. The same applies to new vehicles. Development needs to create good cars, production needs to supply them reliably within the business structure I described earlier, and sales needs to continue selling each vehicle with a focus on its value, as it does today. Our discussion is that, if we can do that, we can overcome the impacts of U.S. tariffs and the situation in the Middle East. By building on these efforts one by one, we would like our engagement with each customer and each vehicle to translate into the final figures. In China, the NEV share

has now reached 65%. We believe it could rise to more than 80% of the overall market toward 2030. Whether Toyota should have exactly the same NEV share as the market is a separate discussion. However, in view of that market change, we need to prepare a corresponding lineup to reliably deliver vehicles to customers in China. On that basis, we are considering models and variants and preparing those vehicles now. Q. Thank you. I would like to ask about the balance, or the thinking, between the organizational changes, the mobility company you aim to become, and the resulting achievement of 20% ROE or a higher level of ROE. With these organizational changes, you are emphasizing manufacturing again through the idea that making things means developing people. At the same time, you appear to envisage generating profits in three broad areas: the new vehicle business, the value chain business just

discussed, and new businesses such as robotics. When considering 20% or a high level of ROE as an outcome, is it possible to approach 20% with businesses centered on manufacturing? Is that your plan? Or, as you work toward becoming a mobility company, will the earnings profile of the new vehicle business also change? Will robotics become a major driver? As you have just said, I understand that the figure itself is an outcome. However, could you provide more detail on which businesses will drive earnings and to what extent? A. (Yoichi Miyazaki) One request I hear from you every time is, “Please provide more detail.” I thought we had provided considerably more this time, but today’s questions have made me feel that we still need to go another level deeper. With so many OEMs around the world, our survival depends on becoming a company customers choose not only for our vehicles, but also for

the experiences and emotional connection that only Toyota can offer. I believe we must remain firmly committed to that. To do so, simply extending what we have done before will not be enough. We need to develop people who do more than follow manuals: people who wrestle with problems themselves, think of new ideas, involve others, and move forward. Naturally, they will sometimes experience setbacks, but training cannot easily teach them how to recover from those setbacks. We need to develop people who can struggle, encounter obstacles, and then pick themselves up again. To open up new businesses and expand the numerator of ROE, we first need to develop people like that. That also connects to the organizational restructuring. At the same time, I believe it is true that, as the company has grown, we have seen more and

more “control, control, control” in the name of governance. We would like to streamline the organization itself while also improving capital efficiency, creating capacity for growth investment and shareholder returns. The organizational changes and the business structure reforms explained today are individual measures we are taking as we step back and review the whole company. Of course, if we tried to explain everything in a single presentation, even we would run out of breath. We would like to continue providing updates, showing you our progress, and discussing suggestions such as, “Would it be better to do this differently here?” To be honest, in the past, even with vehicle sales volumes, part of me felt, “If we disclose that much externally, are we not helping our competitors?” Even now, I struggle with how much we should disclose. However, when we explain our thinking externally

like this, it naturally reaches other companies as well. Precisely for that reason, we need to strengthen ourselves again and be even further advanced the next time we come here. In that sense, we would like to use these exchanges with you as a stimulus for Toyota’s own growth. I hope you will continue to support Toyota’s growth. [END]

• Rebellions plans to adopt NVIDIA NVLink Fusion to connect its next-generation R200 neural processing units to NVIDIA’s open infrastructure platform for rack-scale inference.

• SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems in its AI data center to support its vision for full-stack sovereign AI spanning infrastructure, proprietary models and public-facing services, including those under Korea’s “AI for All” project.
• The collaboration, supported by Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT, aims to connect domestic semiconductor innovation with infrastructure for sovereign AI.

NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom today announced a collaboration to advance Korea’s sovereign AI infrastructure — using NVIDIA NVLink Fusion™ to bring together NVIDIA’s open infrastructure platform, Rebellions’ Korean-designed AI processors and SK Telecom’s AI data center, model and service capabilities.

As part of the agreement, Rebellions will use NVLink Fusion to connect its Rebel R200 neural processing units (NPUs) to the NVIDIA platform, and harness the NVIDIA MGX™ rack architecture for rack-scale system development. SK Telecom plans to deploy these systems, drawing on its AI data center operations expertise, proprietary models and services.

Supported by Korea’s Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), the collaboration aims to support AI services tailored to Korea’s language, industries and priorities, connecting Korean semiconductor development with the systems and operational capabilities needed to deliver AI at scale.

“Korea has the talent, technology and industrial ambition to become a world leader in AI,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Sovereign AI gives nations the power to turn their language, culture and expertise into intelligence. With NVLink Fusion, Korea’s chipmakers can connect their custom ASICs to NVIDIA’s AI factory platform, tightly coupling their processors with NVIDIA compute to run AI workloads. Together with MSIT, Rebellions and SK Telecom, we’re building the computing foundation for Korea to produce its own intelligence and power its next industrial revolution.”

“Today’s announcement marks a turning point, opening a new chapter for sovereign AI by connecting Korea’s AI silicon and models with global systems technology,” said Sunghyun Park, cofounder and CEO of Rebellions. “By integrating Rebellions’ purpose-built silicon and system design with NVIDIA’s NVLink Fusion, high-speed interconnects and rack-scale design expertise, and SKT’s model and data center operations capabilities, we will deliver low-latency and energy-efficient inference for frontier models at scale. As a leading Korean AI silicon startup, we will lead the charge to establish Korean technology as a core pillar powering AI worldwide.”

“This collaboration is meaningful in that it validates the potential of next-generation sovereign AI infrastructure by combining global AI infrastructure technology with Korean AI semiconductors,” said Jung Jai-hun, president and CEO of SK Telecom. “By linking SKT’s AI data centers, proprietary AI models including A.X K2, and public-facing AI services developed under the ‘AI for All’ project, we will strengthen our full-stack sovereign AI competitiveness and contribute to the growth of Korea’s AI ecosystem.”

Scaling Silicon Innovation With NVIDIA’s Open Infrastructure Platform NVLink Fusion extends NVIDIA’s vertically integrated, horizontally open AI platform to custom XPUs. It enables chipmakers to combine specialized silicon with NVIDIA’s high-bandwidth, low-latency scale-up networking and established infrastructure ecosystem, helping improve performance, reduce deployment risk and accelerate time to market.

Rebellions is developing its next-generation R200 NPU, optimized for low-latency and energy-efficient inference using frontier models, including multitrillion-parameter mixture-of-experts models. Through NVLink Fusion, Rebellions will connect its R200 NPUs within a rack through NVIDIA NVLink™ scale-up networking.

The NVIDIA MGX rack architecture and reference designs will support development of the systems, while the MGX ecosystem gives Rebellions access to an established supply chain of original design manufacturers and component suppliers.

Connecting Infrastructure, Models and Services SK Telecom brings experience building and operating AI data centers, alongside its proprietary foundation models and public-facing AI services. Building on its long-standing collaboration with NVIDIA in AI development and sovereign infrastructure, SK Telecom plans to connect these capabilities and deploy them in its AI data center using the standardized MGX rack architecture to deliver full-stack sovereign AI.

The MGX rack architecture provides a foundation for GPU and NPU systems to share data center design elements, including rack footprint, power delivery and cooling. This approach can support infrastructure planning alongside Rebellions’ processor and system development.

The companies plan to develop an approach to disaggregated inference, assigning different stages of AI response generation to the processor architecture best suited to each task. Their planned work includes using NVIDIA GPUs for prefill and Rebellions NPUs for decode to improve inference throughput and power efficiency.

SK Telecom plans to connect this infrastructure with its proprietary foundation models and public-facing services, including those under the government’s AI for All project, to advance its full-stack sovereign AI strategy.

Supporting Sovereign AI Infrastructure With NVLink Fusion MSIT is supporting collaboration between NVIDIA and Korean NPU companies, beginning with Rebellions and SK Telecom, to strengthen Korea’s sovereign AI infrastructure.

“This collaboration with NVIDIA marks a significant step forward, as it enables Korean-developed NPUs to enter the computing infrastructure market alongside NVIDIA, a global leader in AI computing, through NVLink Fusion,” said Bae Kyung-hoon, Korea Deputy Prime Minister, and Minister of Science and Information and Communication Technologies. “The government will actively support this collaboration to deliver tangible results and further advance cooperation with NVIDIA across a range of areas, including physical AI and securing GPU supply.”

By connecting Korean-developed processors and models with NVIDIA infrastructure and SK Telecom’s data center expertise, the companies aim to establish a foundation for sovereign AI services across Korea’s public and private sectors.
Availability Rebellions’ R200 systems are expected to be ready for deployment in 2028.
Micron Announces Over $67 Million in New Idaho Community Investments for Transportation, Housing and Children

BOISE, Idaho, Oct. 27, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Micron Technology, Inc. (Nasdaq: MU) is making over $67 million in new community investments to expand public transportation across the Treasure Valley, improve affordable housing and homeownership opportunities and help Idaho children begin saving at a young age.

In 2023, alongside Idaho Gov. Brad Little and Boise Mayor Lauren McLean, Micron announced its Community Investment Framework to ensure the communities hosting the company’s expansion share in its benefits. The framework focuses on the transportation, housing, workforce and family priorities that matter most to Idahoans. Micron’s $67 million-plus in new investments include:
• Over $45 million to eligible Idaho children via Trump Accounts (also known as 530A Accounts)

These commitments build on the approximately $75 million Micron has contributed to Idaho communities since 2023 through more than 100 grants, investments and partnerships spanning roadway improvements, workforce development, education, STEM and AI programs, housing, childcare and community engagement. Micron’s commitments also include internships, apprenticeships, volunteerism and industry-leading training programs that support students, workers and families while helping build an advanced semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem in the state. More detail about Micron’s prior investments is available here.

“Idaho has been home to Micron for 48 years, and our future here is inseparable from the people and communities who have helped us grow," said April Arnzen, executive vice president, chief people officer and president of the Micron Foundation. "As we expand, we are investing in what matters most to our neighbors: affordable housing, career pathways, easier commutes and a head start on savings for Idaho's children. Together with our community partners, we are committed to ensuring the families who call Idaho home share in the opportunities ahead.”“Idaho’s success has always been built on strong partnerships, and Micron has been a vital partner for nearly half a century,” said Idaho Gov. Brad Little. “Micron’s growth means good-paying jobs for Idahoans, and I appreciate that the company is matching that growth with real investment in the things families feel every day: buying a home, driving to work and giving their kids a strong future with opportunities here at home. Putting money directly into savings accounts for Idaho children is exactly the kind of private-sector leadership that keeps Idaho a great place to live, work and raise a family.”“Companies that call Idaho home have a role to play in helping our working families get ahead,” said Mike Moyle, speaker of the Idaho House of Representatives. “From savings accounts for Idaho kids to housing and transportation, Micron is putting real dollars behind its Idaho roots, and that’s a model I hope other employers in this state will follow.”“Building more homes that Boiseans can afford takes partners who are willing to roll up their sleeves and invest in solutions,” said Boise Mayor Lauren McLean. “Thanks to Micron's investment, we are one step closer to bringing clean geothermal heat to hundreds of affordable homes in Boise. This is what is possible when the city brings public, private and philanthropic partners together around a shared commitment to Boise's future.”

Micron is investing approximately $11.6 million over five years to help Valley Regional Transit (VRT) expand access to public transportation across the Treasure Valley. The investment will establish a new regional bus route connecting Caldwell, Nampa, Meridian and Boise; expand VRT On-Demand service near Micron’s Boise campus; and add Park & Ride locations throughout the region. Together, these improvements will give more residents practical transportation options as Micron continues to expand in Idaho.

Micron is also working closely with the Ada County Highway District (ACHD) and City of Boise to create pathways for private funding for much needed transportation expansions, such as Lake Hazel and Orchard extensions to expedite the construction of these corridors. Micron is also studying further improvements along Interstate 84 together with the Idaho Transportation Department (ITD) and other developers.

Expanding housing and homeownership opportunitiesOver the last decade, mortgages have moved out of reach for many Idahoans. Micron is investing in housing to expand the supply of attainable homes and preserve their long-term affordability.

• $2.5 million in gap funding for the Lusk District Redevelopment Project, a J. Fisher Companies development in partnership with the City of Boise's Housing Land Trust Program, advancing plans for more than 300 new affordable housing units in Boise. The development will use geothermal energy to deliver heat to hundreds of affordable homes.

• $8 million for a partnership with LEAP Housing, including $4 million to add 30 two- and three-bedroom rental homes in Mountain Home, Idaho, and $4 million to support down-payment assistance for up to 200 first-time homebuyers across Ada, Boise, Canyon, Elmore and Gem counties.

In June, Micron announced a $250 million investment to increase long-term savings opportunities for America’s children through Trump Accounts. As part of the commitment, Micron will provide a one-time $250 seed deposit for children with Trump Accounts in locations where the company operates.
In Idaho, Micron expects to deposit over $45 million to more than 181,000 accounts for children under 18 in Ada, Boise, Canyon, Elmore and Gem counties.

Elaine Clegg, CEO, Valley Regional Transit:“Getting people to work, school and everyday destinations is how a growing region stays connected. Micron’s significant $11.6 million investment over five years will expand regional bus services and introduce VRT On-Demand in Boise, giving all residents of the valley a flexible way to get around. As demand increases, transit provides a proven alternative that can reduce the number of vehicles on the road. We are grateful for Micron's partnership, leadership and commitment to our community, and riders will see it on the road with Micron-supported vehicles and services early next year.”

Bart Cochran, CEO, LEAP Housing:“Whether it’s a family looking for a rental they can afford or a young couple trying to buy their first home, Idahoans are eager for housing opportunity. Micron’s $8 million investment will help LEAP build 30 new rental homes in Mountain Home and help up to 200 families across five Idaho counties with down payments on their first homes. Construction can start quickly, which means Idaho families will feel the difference soon.”

Owen Fisher, CEO and Founder, J. Fisher Companies:“Our purpose at J. Fisher Companies is to build places for everyone, and the Lusk District puts that purpose to work in Boise. Micron's $2.5 million investment helps close the funding gap on more than 340 affordable homes close to downtown, so more Idaho families can build their lives in the heart of the city."

Bobbi-Jo Meuleman, President & CEO, Boise Metro Chamber:“For 48 years, Micron has been an important part of Boise’s business community, and its commitment to the region extends far beyond its campus. Through investments in housing, transportation and Idaho families, Micron continues to demonstrate what it means to be a strong community partner. We appreciate Micron’s continued commitment to strengthening our region and creating opportunities for generations to come.”

• Eaton selected for Dassault Falcon 10X to support fuel-efficiency and performance objectives
• Long-standing collaboration brings hydraulic and fuel system technologies to Dassault’s next-generation business jet

CLEVELAND, OH - Intelligent power management company Eaton was selected by Dassault Aviation to provide hydraulic power system and fuel system technologies for the Falcon 10X, the company’s new ultra-long-range business jet. Building on a longstanding collaboration between the two companies, Eaton’s flight-proven technologies and engineering expertise are expected to support aircraft weight, fuel-efficiency and certification objectives ahead of the aircraft’s entry into service.

Eaton’s Hydraulic Power Generation System powers critical aircraft functions, including flight controls, landing gear, braking and steering systems, while providing monitoring and redundancy intended to support safety and reliability objectives. The agreement between Dassault and Eaton also includes system-level modeling, validation activities and a test rig to support Dassault’s system-level European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) certification activities. Eaton also supported ground testing associated with the Falcon 10X’s successful first flight.

“The Falcon 10X is setting a new benchmark in business aviation, and Eaton is proud to help make it possible,” said Armando Tellez, President, Fuel and Motion Control Systems Division. “Our advanced technologies are designed to deliver the performance, reliability and safety that customers expect from industry-leading platforms.”

Eaton fuel system technologies selected for the Falcon 10X build on proven products already deployed across commercial and business aviation platforms. Their established performance can help reduce development complexity, accelerate production readiness and reduce program risk.

For decades, Eaton’s aerospace solutions have maintained a long track record of reliability over countless flight hours across multiple platforms. Utilizing engineering resources from across the world, Eaton will complete the final stages of application-specific development later this year.

Dassault Group is a France-based group of companies established after World War II with the creation of Dassault Aviation by Marcel Dassault, who began building aircraft over 100 years ago. Dassault Aviation, designs and manufactures military aircraft, business jets and space systems, mainly the Rafale fighter and Falcon jets. Since 1965, nearly 2,600 Falcons have been delivered with over 2,200 still in service in over 90 countries.

Eaton is an intelligent power management company dedicated to protecting the environment and improving the quality of life for people everywhere. We make products for the data center, utility, industrial, commercial, machine building, residential, aerospace and mobility markets. We are guided by our commitment to do business right, to operate sustainably and to help our customers manage power ─ today and well into the future. By capitalizing on the global growth trends of electrification and digitalization, we’re helping to solve the world’s most urgent power management challenges and building a more sustainable society for people today and generations to come.

Founded in 1911, Eaton has continuously evolved to meet the changing and expanding needs of our stakeholders. With revenues of $27.4 billion in 2025, the company serves customers in 180 countries. For more information, visit www.eaton.com. Follow us on LinkedIn.

SOUTHFIELD, Mich.— Intelligent power management company Eaton today announced that its Mobility segment is expanding its ELocker® differential portfolio with the introduction of next-generation Dana 60 and Dana 80 applications. These products will debut at the Specialty Equipment Market Association (SEMA) Show, Nov. 3-6 in Las Vegas. The new designs feature Eaton’s first Dana 80 ELocker and a new 4-pinion architecture providing a platform for future ELocker portfolio growth.

The next-generation designs improve durability, strength and overall product robustness for demanding applications. Key features include a ramp-style design, reinforced thrust washer with increased surface area, larger lock collar, upgraded cross-shaft, strengthened cast-iron case and additional ring gear bolt support.
• Dana 60 4-Pinion ELocker®: Rear axle applications featuring a 9.75" ring gear, 35-spline shafts, and 4.10 & dn and 4.56 & up gear ratios.
• Dana 80 4-Pinion ELocker®: Rear axle applications featuring an 11.5" ring gear, 40-spline shafts, and 4.10 & up gear ratios.
“Built by enthusiasts for enthusiasts, the new Dana 60 ELocker reflects Eaton's commitment to product innovation driven by real-world feedback and experience.”
The new applications are scheduled to begin shipping in March 2027.

The current Dana 60 ELocker remains Eaton’s recommended solution and will continue to be fully supported. There are no immediate changes to product availability, ordering or customer support. What’s the News? AMD is advancing the AMD Instinct™ MI400 Series GPU portfolio with updates spanning scientific computing and AI. AMD is sharing additional details on AMD Instinct™ MI430X GPUs for high-performance computing and AI for science, alongside new measured inference results for the AMD Instinct™ MI455X GPU on the AMD Helios™ rackscale solution. AMD is also introducing the AMD Instinct™ MI450X GPU, giving AMD Helios customers another option to match memory capacity with their AI workloads and deployment needs.

Why It Matters? Scientific simulation, frontier AI and interactive inference place different demands on infrastructure. MI400 Series GPUs address those needs with native double-precision compute for scientific applications, high-capacity memory for demanding AI models and additional configuration choices.

How Does MI430X Support Scientific Computing? The AMD Instinct MI430X GPU is designed for workloads that bring together high-precision simulation and AI. Its native FP64 capabilities support demanding scientific calculations, while 432 gigabytes (GB) of HBM4 memory and up to 23.3 terabytes per second of memory bandwidth help researchers work with larger simulations and datasets.

AMD is sharing a closer look at the role of native double precision in scientific computing. New AMD research examines 47 workload configurations across 11 applications and benchmarks, exploring where FP64 emulation can help and where scientific codes depend on native double-precision compute. The findings reinforce the focus on supporting the varied computational demands of HPC and AI for science with the AMD Instinct MI430X GPU.
More: "Exascale Was the Beginning: AMD Instinct MI430X GPUs"

How Is MI455X Advancing AI Performance? New AMD testing demonstrates leadership inference performance on MI455X powering AMD Helios delivering 21,333 tokens per second per GPU on DeepSeek-R1 using an MLPerf Inference Offline configuration – resulting in up to 30% higher throughput than the Nvidia Vera Rubin latest published MLPerf offline result.1

AMD Helios further extends its infrastructure leadership with up to 20% higher HBM bandwidth2 and higher scale-up bandwidth than Nvidia Vera Rubin,3 enabling the inference performance demonstrated in these results.

What is the MI450X? AMD is expanding the AMD Instinct MI400 Series portfolio with the new AMD Instinct MI450X GPU, giving AMD Helios customers greater flexibility with an additional choice to match their AI workloads and deployment needs. MI450X offers 288 GB of HBM4 memory per GPU while delivering the same core compute, memory bandwidth and scale-up and scale-out connectivity capabilities as MI455X.

Built on the AMD flexible compute architecture and open foundation, MI450X illustrates how AMD quickly responds to evolving customer requirements while streamlining bring-up and integration for ecosystem partners.

For workloads that fit within its memory capacity, MI450X provides another option to meet throughput and response-time targets while optimizing operating expenses. For AMD Helios deployments, customers can select MI450X or MI455X GPUs, with both supported by the same open rack-scale architecture and AMD ROCm™ software foundation, while the MI455X GPU provides additional memory headroom for larger models, longer contexts or higher concurrency.

Intel announced a collaboration with RadixArk to optimize SGLang, an open-source AI inference stack, for Intel platforms that aims to help developers and enterprises deploy leading AI models and build AI applications more efficiently and cost-effectively.

Enterprise AI is moving beyond isolated performance benchmarks to solving full-system production deployments. This collaboration ensures developers have Day-0 readiness and high-performance inference software directly optimized for Intel CPUs, GPUs and accelerators with an open approach and gives them the freedom to choose the tools, frameworks and technologies that best fit their needs.
vice president, AI Products & GTM, Intel Data Center Group

Enterprises require heterogeneous, open inference infrastructure, as AI models grow larger and more complex. To deliver AI in production it requires that every prompt is routed to the right place, matching the different workloads with the right intelligence, right compute and right economics. Open inference runtimes provide the essential connective tissue that makes full-stack deployments practical, reliable, and economically sustainable across diverse enterprise environments.

This collaboration expands developer choice to deploy leading AI models on enterprise-proven Intel hardware. Model builders and software engineers can build and innovate on standard, open frameworks and interfaces while taking full advantage of Intel’s compute density and built-in hardware acceleration features, including Intel Advanced Matrix Extensions (Intel AMX). Developers gain faster time-to-production, reduced latency, and flexible deployment options across existing data center and cloud capacity.

"Our collaboration with Intel is a major milestone for open-source AI inference, enabling SGLang optimization directly to Intel’s platforms. By upstreaming deep optimizations into the core framework, we are eliminating constraints and ensuring developers never have to compromise between open standards and high performance. Our mission to make frontier AI infrastructure open and accessible to every builder, and Intel’s enterprise-ready architecture gives development teams the flexibility and compute density they need to scale production AI workloads seamlessly."
An Open Blueprint for Production AI

Bringing hardware and software optimization together reflects Intel’s approach of contributing improvements directly to community software, rather than treating them as separate deployment decisions. These upstream contributions to popular engines and frameworks aim to provide high-performance paths for turning breakthrough models into scalable, production-grade applications while preserving flexibility, choice and broad architectural freedom.

SANTA CLARA, Calif., November 10 – Intel and Altera today announced a collaboration to develop a flexible, real-time sensor bridge for a range of Edge & Physical AI industries including healthcare, aerospace and defense, and robotics applications. By combining Intel compute, connectivity and software with Altera FPGAs, the companies aim to help original equipment manufacturers (OEMs) address the growing complexity of connecting, processing and acting on real-world data across increasingly sensor-rich edge environments.
Addressing the complexity of sensor-rich edge systems

Edge and Physical AI systems can require data from different sensors and interfaces to be brought together while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost. Some applications also require very high bandwidth or flexible form factors in which input/output (I/O) is located away from the compute board. Sensor data must then be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use across edge, robotics and other workloads.

Intel and Altera plan to address these challenges through modular reference solutions that combine programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation. The goal is to give OEMs greater flexibility as applications, sensors and workloads evolve, while helping them move more efficiently from prototype to deployment.

As sensors multiply at the edge and through Physical AI systems, our customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action. Together with Altera, we aim to give OEMs a flexible foundation that simplifies integration and helps them move faster from prototype to market deployment while meeting their needs across performance, power and cost
corporate vice president and general manager, Edge Computing Group, Intel

Physical AI systems have to sense, decide, and act in real time, and the physical world demands accuracy, reliability, and safety. Altera FPGAs provide the sensor connectivity, data processing, and deterministic control that machines need to respond to the physical world, and they stay programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Combining that with Intel’s compute and software is intended to give OEMs a flexible foundation to tailor systems to their needs
head of business solutions and marketing at Altera
Applying programmable, real-time processing across edge markets

Intel and Altera plan to apply the collaboration across multiple markets where real-time processing and programmable computing matter most. These capabilities will be accessible to developers through Intel’s Open Edge Platform SDK and an Altera SDK.
• Healthcare: The companies are jointly developing a reference solution targeting the stringent latency and real-time requirements of advanced healthcare equipment.

• Aerospace and defense: Intel and Altera are collaborating on reference solutions for next-generation mission systems, with a focus on size, weight and power requirements for converged AI and signal-processing workloads.

• Robotics: Intel and Altera plan to combine Intel compute, connectivity and robotics software with Altera FPGA technology to help address the increasingly complex sensing, timing and real-time processing requirements of intelligent machines.

Together, Intel and Altera aim to help OEMs move faster from prototype to deployment with programmable real-time sensor bridge reference solutions that are designed to reduce integration complexity while addressing performance, power and cost requirements across a range of edge applications.

Intel (Nasdaq: INTC) designs and manufactures advanced semiconductors that connect and power the modern world. Every day, our engineers create new technologies that enhance and shape the future of computing to enable new possibilities for every customer we serve. Learn more at intel.com.

Altera provides high-performance, programmable compute and connectivity solutions that enable the rapid adoption and continued advancement of transformative technologies across a wide range of advanced and AI-enabled systems. Altera is the largest pure-play FPGA provider with a full-spectrum portfolio serving applications ranging from data centers and communications networks to critical embedded systems.

Samsung Electronics today announced the upcoming launch of the full lineup of intelligent eyewear, delivering a smarter way to see the world through intuitive, hands-free AI assistance. Set for release in the U.S. and South Korea on Dec. 10 with pre-orders beginning today, the collection combines Samsung’s mobile engineering expertise with 30 distinctive designs1 from Gentle Monster and Warby Parker for comfortable, stylish everyday wear. Developed in collaboration with Google and with Gemini built in, the intelligent eyewear helps users understand the world around them, communicate across languages and stay connected while remaining present in the moment. Responsibly designed with everyone’s comfort in mind, the intelligent eyewear has controls that put the user in charge and has privacy protections for both the wearer and people around them.
Designed for Style and Everyday Comfort

Gentle Monster and Warby Parker bring their design identities to a combined lineup of 30 designs, offering customers a wide range of frame shapes, colors, sizes, and lens treatments to match their personal style. Gentle Monster brings bold, disruptive aesthetics, while Warby Parker offers timeless designs with a refined appeal.

Samsung’s engineering expertise brings together the advanced hardware required for intelligent eyewear in slim, lightweight frames without sacrificing durability or comfort. Weighing around 41 grams,2 the eyewear was carefully designed to balance weight, structural strength, and comfort, making it suitable for extended use throughout the day.
More Intuitive Ways To Interact With the World
With Gemini built in, the intelligent eyewear provides intuitive, hands-free experiences. It is designed to help users stay connected and present while offering a range of capabilities:

• Explore and understand surroundings: Users can ask questions about what they see3 — such as identifying an unfamiliar landmark or learning about an object — continuing the conversation naturally with follow-up questions.

• Enhance daily productivity: The intelligent eyewear helps users turn information into action. For example, a user can capture a whiteboard during a meeting, ask Gemini to summarize the key takeaways and save them directly into Samsung Notes.
• Translate and navigate on the go:4 Users can translate a restaurant menu or find their way around unfamiliar places with turn-by-turn directions from Google Maps.

• Stay connected, hands-free: The intelligent eyewear allows users to effortlessly stay connected. It can automatically prioritize, group, and summarize notifications based on context, read important updates aloud and enable natural voice responses. Whether making calls or responding to messages while their hands are occupied, users can stay connected on the go.

Behind these intelligent experiences is purpose-built hardware to support natural, hands-free interactions. A 12MP HDR camera provides visual context for Gemini while supporting high-resolution photos and clear video recording. Open-ear speakers and a four-microphone array enable clear voice interactions, calls and audio playback while maintaining awareness of the user’s surroundings.

Powered by the Snapdragon® AR1 Gen 1 Platform,5 the intelligent eyewear delivers smooth performance with up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge, and up to 72 hours with a fully charged charging case.6 Designed to work in tandem with Galaxy phones, the intelligent eyewear utilizes a split-computing system to offload a portion of the processing load to the connected device. This approach, combined with Samsung’s careful optimization of component placement, battery design, and thermal management, helps balance performance, durability and everyday comfort in a lightweight form factor.

The intelligent eyewear was responsibly designed with the comfort and privacy of everyone in mind, recognizing the need to consider both the people wearing it and those around them. This commitment has shaped key decisions from the outset, with transparency and user control built into the experience.
Responsible design is built into the practical experience:

• Clear recording indicators: When capturing images or recording video for your gallery, an LED indicates that the camera is active, while the wearer simultaneously receives a visual notification via an inner light and a sound. Built-in safeguards are designed to disable camera capture if the external LED is covered or not functioning properly.

• Considerate audio design: Open-ear speakers are designed to minimize sound leakage while helping wearers remain aware of their surroundings. In conversations with Gemini Live, surrounding sounds, including other people’s voices, are filtered to help protect bystander privacy.

• User control and data privacy: Users retain control over both app-specific permissions and their Gemini activity. Visuals collected by Gemini are not used for AI model training or ad targeting. When users ask Gemini about what they’re looking at, the intelligent eyewear is designed to automatically redact bystanders’ faces before responding.
• Responsible use: The intelligent eyewear is designed for users aged 18 and over, with age verification required for device activation and app downloads.
For more detailed information on the privacy policies for the intelligent eyewear, please visit Google’s privacy blog post.
